titleSource: Chapter 6: Social Media Is for Growth

sittings.bodyEn: After the first customers pay, this chapter turns them into a small circle that will support the next project too. A hundred people who know you and trust you will usually out-earn ten thousand people who never reply. The picture is a charity ride: a plain ask to an existing audience raised about thirty thousand dollars in three days, and almost every donor was someone already helped in public. The money followed years of free teaching, advice, and simple encouragement, with no invoice attached. Generosity is the method, and the ask comes only after that relationship is real. A huge quiet following is a weak substitute for the circle.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean the few people who already share your problem and will pay attention.
If they say this, they mean people who trust you enough to show up when you finally ask.

sittings.bodyEn: The audience here began as a public diary for old friends, then tightened around starting a business because readers kept asking. Failures stayed in the record, and that openness is what later made introductions possible. People follow a character they can recognize, and they buy from someone who feels like a friend. You can share before a polished brand exists. Honesty about a specific interest is the advantage. A lawn crew that posts short before-and-after clips for nearby homeowners shows the same lesson, because the work itself can be the character.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean showing the work, including the misses, so people can follow a real person.

sittings.bodyEn: Before you publish, answer why a stranger should care, in about thirty seconds. The answer has four parts: who you are, why someone should trust you, what you care about, and what that history prepares you to do for them. A strength coach in the chapter found his after a pause: years with elite athletes, a love of helping people perform, and a promise to share the mindset he had watched up close. The early lines say what makes you specific, and the last line says the help you will give. Write the pitch in a journal, and expect to change it, because there is no single correct version. You still need one before the first post, specific enough that the wrong people can leave.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean a thirty-second pitch with who you are, why you are credible, what you love, and how you help.

sittings.bodyEn: Social reach in this chapter is free, and you start on exactly one platform as an experiment. Choose with three tests: where your buyers already spend time, which format you will enjoy making, and where an hour of work returns the most useful attention. A platform that fails those tests for you can still be right for someone whose buyers live there. The pass in the chapter is video, because the audience is huge, hosting costs nothing, and harder production means fewer competitors. A phone in a living room is enough, and you can grow without showing your face. Point the profile toward the email list you will build next.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean a single free channel chosen for the audience, the format, and the return on an hour.
If they say this, they mean attention or trust you get back for each hour of making.

sittings.bodyEn: Take the four-part angle and rewrite the bio on the one platform you chose. Say who you are and how you help the customer you want, in language a stranger can repeat. Cut titles that could describe anyone. The short model in the chapter names the company, an old role, and the place where the help lives. Do this cleanup before you open a second network. Later posts should sound like the same person the bio just introduced.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean the bio rewritten from your angle so a stranger knows how you help.

sittings.bodyEn: A medical student grew a very large channel by teaching one entrance exam, section by section, to people who needed that exact help. The content circle starts that narrow, on a niche inside a niche, as long as you and they both care. The middle ring overlaps the core and speaks wider, the way exam tips widened into studying for students in general. The outer ring is the biggest topic that still includes the original people, such as income or tools that came from the same work. Fish-tank reviews, a small biohacking channel that sells through affiliates, and backyard chicken meetups follow the same widening. Write each ring as the outcome you deliver plus the people you serve.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean topics that start tiny and widen only while the original people still see themselves.
If they say this, they mean the smallest group and the one outcome you serve first.

sittings.bodyEn: After the rings are named, find a point of view inside them. Ask what your market treats as true that you think is wrong. Ask what they should be talking about and are not. Ask which mistakes they keep making without noticing. The piece should be relevant, useful, and a little surprising, and it should feel like a journey they take with you. A cleaning business in the chapter moves from cooler care in one hot region, to detergent for new homeowners, to vacuums for families. Write those three rings before you record anything.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean the formula for a ring: the result you deliver and the people it is for.

sittings.bodyEn: Audiences in this chapter do not want a lecture from someone who pretends to have the finished answer. They want a guide who is still in the work. Show what you did, including the awkward parts, and frame it as your process. A tow-truck channel documents an ordinary job and still teaches, because the steps are visible. Invite people to dare you, correct you, or object, and then answer them in public. Their replies improve the work and give the platform a reason to spread it. Some of the most watched pieces are the ones where the attempt fails.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean you document your own process, including misses, instead of lecturing from a finished rule.
If they say this, they mean letting the audience dare you, correct you, or object, then answering in public.

sittings.bodyEn: Publish one piece today on the platform you chose. Use the angle, the core circle, and a point of view, and let the format be a video, a thread, or a post. Skip the studio, the perfect script, and the view count for this rep. This public step is the start of the community, and the piece is allowed to look ordinary. You already wrote the ingredients on the earlier pages. Fix the format on the next one. The following chapter moves this attention onto an email list you control.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean the piece that exists today, however plain it looks.

sittings.bodyEn: This chapter builds a small circle before it builds a crowd. Write who you are, why you are credible, what you care about, and what you will do for people. Choose one free platform using your buyers, a format you will keep making, and a decent return on an hour. Start with a narrow outcome, widen only in rings that still include those people, and post as a guide who shows the real process. One public piece starts the community, however plain it looks. A quiet crowd that never replies is the result this chapter is trying to avoid.
sittings.prompt: What should be true before you chase a bigger audience?
choices: You have a four-part angle, one platform, a narrow outcome, and one public piece
You have opened five networks and copied whatever is trending
You have bought followers so the profile looks established
You have waited until the gear and the script feel finished
